passage: At the cooperative bank in the small town, the shutters came down at four, but the ledgers stayed open till eight. Asif had finished the day's entries by half past four. He opened the ledger again and checked pages he had already checked. Kavitha, the senior clerk, was still tapping at her calculator, and Prakash, the peon, sipped his third tea. Nobody looked at the clock. Asif thought of the 5.45 bus he was missing yet again. "If I leave first, they will think I do not care," he told himself, and took the last auto home at nine.

qa.q: When had Asif finished the day's entries?
qa.a: Asif had finished the day's entries by half past four.

qa.q: Why does Asif stay at the bank when the work is done?
qa.a: Asif fears looking less committed if he leaves first, so he is anxious about being judged; the worry is about how others see him, not about the ledgers.

qa.q: What small step could Asif take to test whether the late evenings are really needed?
qa.a: Asif could ask Kavitha which task truly needs the evening hours, or leave on time one day with a friendly word.

qa.q: What might Kavitha be thinking while she taps at the calculator long after closing?
qa.a: Kavitha may have real work left, or may be following the same custom without asking; nothing in the scene shows that anyone has questioned it.

grounding: A young professional stays late because everyone does, though the work is done, and fears seeming less committed.

passage: By four o'clock Ines had sent the report, but in the Lisbon open-plan office jackets still hung over chairs like little flags. Emil ate a sandwich at his desk and murmured, "One more thing," though his screen was blank. Marta, the team head, was on a long call with her door open. At five Tomas quietly packed his bag and left, and two people glanced at his empty chair. Ines opened an old spreadsheet and scrolled without reading. She wondered whether anyone truly needed her at seven, and whether anyone would say so if she asked.

qa.q: What hung over the chairs in the Lisbon office?
qa.a: Jackets hung over the chairs like little flags.

qa.q: What is Ines worried about while scrolling the old spreadsheet?
qa.a: Ines worries about looking less committed than the others, and doubts whether staying is needed at all.

qa.q: What could Ines ask or try instead of scrolling through an old spreadsheet?
qa.a: Ines could ask Marta which work really needs evening hours, or leave on time once and see what actually happens.

qa.q: How might Tomas have felt when leaving at five while two people glanced at his chair?
qa.a: Tomas may have felt a little self-conscious but settled enough to go; packing quietly and leaving suggests he had decided the work was done.

grounding: A young professional stays late because everyone does though the work is done, and rarely asks whether the norm serves anyone.

passage:
The branch of the cooperative bank in the town closed its counters at four. By half past five Gargi had finished the day's entries, tallied her cash and even filed next week's forms.
Nobody moved. The manager's cabin light was on. Sabina at the next desk was slowly scrolling through a ledger she had already checked. The peon made another round of tea.
Gargi thought of the last bus to her village at seven and her mother waiting with dinner. She picked up her bag, then put it down again. Last month a clerk who left at six had been called “part-timer” for a week.
At seven-fifteen the manager finally stood up. Everyone stood. Gargi took an autorickshaw home she could barely afford.

qa.q: When did the counters close?
qa.a: The counters closed at four.

qa.q: Why did Gargi put her bag down again?
qa.a: She felt afraid of being judged as less committed, like the clerk who left at six and was called a "part-timer" for a week.

qa.q: What small step could Gargi take about the late evenings?
qa.a: She could ask the manager whether staying is really needed once the work is done, or agree with Sabina to leave together on time.

qa.q: How might Sabina be experiencing these evenings?
qa.a: Sabina seems to be pretending to work too, slowly scrolling a ledger she already checked, so she may feel just as stuck.

grounding: Shows a young professional staying late because everyone does though her work is done, fearing she will look less committed.

passage:
At the insurance firm in Johannesburg, the fifth floor emptied only when Mr Botha did. Lindiwe knew that by her second week.
Her sister's birthday dinner was at seven. At six her claims were done. She looked at Mina, who was also staring at a finished spreadsheet.
“You going?” Lindiwe whispered.
“Are you?” Mina whispered back.
Neither moved. Across the room, Thabo was pretending to read emails. The cleaner began vacuuming around their chairs.
Lindiwe texted her sister: running late, sorry, start without me. At eight Mr Botha put on his coat and said, “Good work, team.” Lindiwe smiled and nodded, and in the lift she wondered whether he even noticed who stayed.

qa.q: What time was her sister's birthday dinner?
qa.a: It was at seven.

qa.q: What was Lindiwe feeling when she whispered to Mina?
qa.a: She felt anxious and hesitant, wanting to leave for the dinner but afraid to be the first to go.

qa.q: What would you advise Lindiwe and Mina to try?
qa.a: They could agree to leave together when their work is done, or ask Mr Botha directly what he expects, instead of guessing.

qa.q: How might her sister have felt receiving the text?
qa.a: She was probably disappointed and a bit hurt that Lindiwe missed the start of her birthday dinner for no clear reason.

grounding: Shows a young professional staying late only because everyone does, fearing looking less committed and not asking whether it helps anyone.

passage:
The research institute's lab corridor stayed bright till nine every night. Bidisha's samples were in the freezer by five-thirty and her notes were typed.
Gopika, from the next bench, whispered, “Dr Sen walks past at eight. He likes to see faces.”
So Bidisha opened a paper she had already read. Three other assistants did the same. The only sound was the hum of the fridges.
At eight, Dr Sen passed, nodded at the full benches, and left without a word.
Bidisha packed up at eight-thirty. Her back ached. On the auto home she thought about the question she had never asked anyone: did Dr Sen actually want this, or were they all just copying each other? She fell asleep before she could answer it.

qa.q: When did Dr Sen walk past?
qa.a: Dr Sen walked past at eight.

qa.q: What does Bidisha's unanswered question suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels tired and doubtful, suspecting the late hours may be pointless, but too uneasy to ask anyone.

qa.q: How could the lab team find out whether staying late helps?
qa.a: One of them could simply ask Dr Sen what he expects, or the assistants could agree to try leaving on time for a week.

qa.q: How might Gopika see the evening routine?
qa.a: Gopika seems to accept it as how the lab works and passes the rule on as a helpful tip without questioning it.

grounding: Shows a young professional staying late because everyone does though her work is finished, without asking whether the norm helps anyone.

passage:
Himani,
You asked why I never make it to Thursday badminton anymore. Honest answer: I finish my reports by six, and then I sit at my desk until almost nine, pretending to reread them.
Nobody told me to. Farhan, our team lead, stays. Nisha and Arjun stay. The lights stay on. The one evening I packed up at six-thirty, Arjun said "Half day?" with a grin, and I replayed it the whole ride home.
I keep thinking that if I'm the first to leave, they'll decide I'm not serious about the job. The strange part is that nobody seems to do much after seven. Farhan scrolls on his phone, Nisha orders snacks, Arjun watches cricket clips with the sound off.
I've never once asked whether any of us actually needs to be there. Maybe I should.
Save me a court next Thursday? I'll try.
Lalit

qa.q: By what time does Lalit finish the reports?
qa.a: Lalit finishes the reports by six.

qa.q: What worry keeps Lalit at the desk until almost nine?
qa.a: Lalit is anxious that leaving first will make the team think Lalit is not serious, a fear sharpened by Arjun's "Half day?" joke.

qa.q: What small step could Lalit try to test whether staying late is really needed?
qa.a: Lalit could ask Farhan plainly what is expected once the work is done, or leave at six on a finished day and notice what actually happens.

qa.q: How might Himani see Lalit's missed badminton evenings after reading this?
qa.a: Himani may feel a bit let down at first, then realise Lalit is stuck in a habit driven by worry, not by work.

grounding: Illustrates a young professional who stays late only because the whole team does, fearing looking uncommitted and never questioning whether the habit helps anyone.
